news.title: Dangerous gamble: Iran’s evolving missiles get closer to US warships. What changed?
news.text: Dubai: Iran has spent much of its six-month war with the United States trying to make the Strait of Hormuz dangerous for commercial shipping. Now it is taking a far bigger risk: Firing increasingly sophisticated missiles directly at American warships..At least three times in the past week, Iranian forces have launched missiles at US naval vessels, including an aircraft carrier, in attacks that produced much closer calls than previous attempts, according to The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the incidents..US Central Command said the American vessels successfully evaded the attacks..But US officials are increasingly concerned that Iran has improved its ability to track and target moving warships — a difficult military task that requires locating a vessel and continuously updating its position as a missile approaches..So what has changed, and why is Tehran willing to risk a devastating US response?.US-Iran ship attacks open dangerous new phase in battle for Strait of Hormuz.Missiles that can change course.One important difference appears to be the weapons Iran is using..The recent attacks involved medium-range ballistic missiles equipped with manoeuvrable warheads, according to the Journal..Unlike a conventional ballistic warhead following a largely predictable trajectory towards a fixed target, such systems can manoeuvre during flight, potentially allowing them to pursue a moving target..Iran has recently highlighted its Qassem Basir ballistic missile, which Tehran says has improved accuracy and can strike moving targets. It has not been independently established that the missile was used in all the recent attacks on US ships..Whatever the precise weapon involved, American officials believe the closer calls suggest Iran’s targeting capabilities may have improved..Trump’s new 3-pronged strategy: Escort ships, bomb Iran, squeeze Tehran.How is Iran finding moving US ships?.That is perhaps the biggest unanswered question..Hitting a moving warship is far harder than striking a fixed target, requiring accurate tracking and the ability to update the vessel’s position as the missile closes in..Even an advanced missile needs sufficiently accurate information about where a warship is located before it can successfully engage a moving target..US officials are examining whether Iran may be receiving targeting assistance from Russia or China, according to the Journal. There has been no public evidence establishing that either country helped Iran with the recent attacks..The possibility nevertheless worries Washington because better surveillance, satellite imagery or other intelligence could make Iranian missiles substantially more dangerous to US naval forces..How US used Navy divers, underwater drones to clear Strait of Hormuz mines.Why take such a huge risk?.Because Iran is running out of easier ways to change the course of the war..A large US naval force is enforcing a blockade that has severely restricted Iran’s ability to export oil, depriving Tehran of its principal source of foreign currency..US sanctions are adding to the pressure, while Iran’s currency has plunged and inflation has soared..“Iran is escalating because they don’t see other options,” Marc Sievers, a former US ambassador to Oman, told the Journal..The strategy does not require Iran to defeat the vastly more powerful US Navy..Instead, Tehran can try to make maintaining the blockade increasingly expensive and dangerous..Every missile attack forces American vessels to defend themselves, potentially consuming costly interceptors. It also forces Washington repeatedly to decide how much risk it is prepared to accept to keep ships operating close to Iran..US Admiral Cooper's message to IRGC: 'Shoot at two of our ships, lose three of yours'.A dangerous calculation.But there is an enormous difference between firing at an American warship and actually hitting one..A successful strike causing major damage or US casualties could trigger a fierce American response and send the conflict back into full-scale warfare..Yet Iran may see leverage even in that danger..Damaging a US vessel could shake financial markets, alarm Gulf states and confront President Donald Trump with an uncomfortable choice: Retaliate heavily and risk another escalation, or respond more cautiously and face accusations of weakness..That calculation has become even more sensitive with the US midterm elections less than two months away..Tankers for warships.Washington has already demonstrated the price Iran could pay..After Iranian ballistic missiles targeted US naval vessels, American forces began attacking Iranian oil tankers. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has made the policy explicit: attempts to strike US warships will cost Tehran tankers..Iran has responded by widening its own attacks..The Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that they targeted 10 vessels around Hormuz after US attacks on Iranian tankers. Iran also launched missiles at a US base in Jordan..The result is an increasingly dangerous cycle: Iran targets US warships; Washington attacks Iran’s oil lifeline; Tehran retaliates against more ships and military targets..Why Hormuz remains Iran’s strongest card.For all the damage Iran has suffered, geography still gives Tehran leverage..The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world’s most important energy corridors. Washington can destroy missile launchers, escort merchant vessels and move its warships farther offshore, but permanently removing Iran’s ability to threaten shipping is far more difficult..That helps explain why Tehran appears willing to take greater risks there even as its economy comes under mounting pressure..The gamble is extraordinary..Iran cannot match the United States ship for ship or missile for missile. But if its weapons are becoming capable of getting closer to American warships, Tehran does not need to win a naval battle to change Washington’s calculations..It only needs to make every US ship operating around Hormuz a more dangerous — and potentially more politically costly — proposition.
news.summary: Why Iran missiles are getting closer to US warships

news.title: Have the Brits tamed Andy Burnham?
news.text:
Have the Brits tamed their politicians and leadership as well? It’s the intended question and, of course, the first among British politicians is Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Do citizens now prefer political leaders bent on acting like everyday folks to those that concentrate on doing what leaders are universally expected to do – lead? For generals who lead soldiers on battlefields, we know the answers. As for civilians in the UK, whom Burnham is eager to please, we aren’t sure anymore, hence the question. A close look at Burnham’s moves shows he’s determined to meet the expectations of every citizen, giving off the feeling that he’ll try to meet even more expectations if there are, and this disposition raises questions. One: where do we draw the line between what a national leader should be and what people expect him to be? Where does the leader draw a line between being everybody’s man and being the leader? Both questions provide an opportunity to interrogate the trend among politicians in Western democracies who adopt a somewhat anti-establishment and supposedly pro-people approach (populism). Some simply harness and ride on popular sentiments, raising hope, making promises that get them the vote, though they know half of the promises made won’t be fulfilled.

There were years in the past when one could tell what political parties and politicians in Western democracies would promise and what they wouldn’t. They were moderate, keeping their criticisms of ruling parties moderate, conscious that they would arrive in power and that unrealistic promises shown for what they are. So opposition parties largely played responsible not divisive politics, refusing to raise false hopes or make wild promises just to be different. This has changed. Parties and politicians pick any issue that’s as wild as the imagination can get, campaign on it, thereby polarising Western democracies in a way never experienced before. It’s one reason a political party, Alternative for Germany, that won the latest state election has been described as “dangerous” because it’s far-right. Yet the party doesn’t only win; nationally it’s the most popular. I’m not referencing populism for the first time on this page. I raised it back in 2016 after US President Donald Trump rode into the White House on the back of popular sentiments that other US presidential candidates wouldn’t consider or make promises about. As a journalist with political science background, the long term effects of such phenomenon in Western democracies had been of interest to me.

As Trump and his campaign advisers realised back then, populism was the only way they could beat established politicians so it was the path they trod. However, before the age of populism, the kind seen theses days, politicians had been promising something to everyone. Former US President Bill Clinton, in order to win, made campaign promises he later turned away from in his eight years in office. Clinton soon discovered that seeing issues one way outside the White House is different from how one sees them in the White House. Many politicians have experienced a similar situation. Meanwhile, at the time Trump was making populist promises, I pointed out here that the businessman cum politician was following in the footsteps of populist politicians in Europe who had latched on to some of the wilder expectations among citizens. When his margin of winning seemed narrow in late 2015, his men worked on the electorates on the fringes. These were targeted with things like disappearing messages on their personal digital devices.

Such disappearing messages got people mad enough to want to vote against the Democratic Party candidate, as the public controversy surrrounding the activity of the consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, later revealed. Trump won in 2015. But his populist approach would bring in greater dividends in the November 2024 presidential election. However, unlike Trump, who has tested an approach that works and is consolidating in his second tenure, the current UK prime minister hasn’t come into office through the general election route. With Burnham’s party behind in the polls, he’s conducting himself to be liked ahead of the next general election, trying so much to please everyone in a way that appears forced. Having been an actor (and later a playwright) long before I came into journalism, I know there’s something actors call “overacting”. What the prime minister is doing seems needlessly high-octane, reactive, scripted and acted, rather than natural.

It shouldn’t be assumed one doesn’t understand Burnham’s effort to conduct himself like everyday folks. The approach was something I had praised the former PM, Boris Johnson, for. Johnson in his shorts regularly jogged or rode his bicycle across town in the UK essentially to keep fit; he kept the habit even after he became foreign secretary, jogging on streets in New York City when he was there on official UN engagements. I rate that as an unforced approach to being like everyday folks. Johnson had always been doing his own thing, living it simple, long before he came into public office. Add this to his informal approach to official matters – no airs, no loads – just the likeable Johnson who got things done, and the reader would understand why I wrote close to fifty pieces (columns and satires) on him on this page and elsewhere. His relaxed carriage and his looks (face and hair), coupled with his naturally ebullient disposition, come across more as unforced and unscripted Johnson. 

While one doesn’t condemn Burnham for his effort to be approachable if he thinks it’s the best, it needs to be pointed out that he hasn’t contested a general election for this post, so he doesn’t know what works or if his approach will even cut it for the electorate.

Before he’ll know it, his effort at being approachable might have stripped the highest political office in the land of everything presidential without attracting the intended votes. It might have stripped all the fine lines (different from aloofness or haughtiness) that attend leadership. Worse, his approach can encourage extreme expectations (in Western democracies that traditionally avoid extremes), create more disenchantment among citizens when expectations aren’t met, become a source of instability as well as disaffection with the electoral process, and ultimately undermine democracy. Such is the point of the reality check this piece is about.

It’s worth noting that while politicians traditionally avoid extremes, a populist approach has produced “far-right” and “far-left” political parties once abhorred in the West. I think efforts to please everyone, such as Burnham is doing, can end up producing the same outcome for which “far-right” and “far-left” politicians and their parties are feared. This is the core of this piece. From his first day in Number 10, Downing Street, Burnham sends out the signal he wants to make citizens feel he’s one of them. He said he would take things out of government offices in London, and devolve power to city and town councils. He’s shown that unlike his immediate predecessor, he won’t always stay behind podiums making speeches. So, he’s been going to pubs drinking beer, as well as engaging in other similar informal activities. Burnham’s informal interactions are so many in the short period he’s been in office that they can beat the entire informal outings of some past PMs who spent a longer time in power. One isn’t certain that’s the hallmark of leadership, but if it brings people closer in the age of populism, it can pass, except that other issues of immediate concern tend to be the determinants when the electorate votes, not how affable a political leader is. And there’s no better example to cite here than Trump; he doesn’t concern himself with going to pubs or dressing like everyday folks, yet he maintains his core base of political supporters. Reason? He shows leadership on issues that matter to his voters.

There are choices Burnham has to make regarding his leadership style, and with the condition of people in the UK I don’t think emphasising the likeable, simple-fellow approach to win every voter’s heart is one of them. The things that bother citizens are more serious in nature than that. Burnham’s immediate predecessor, Keir Starmer, might have been perceived as stiff and formal (and I pointed this out in my satires long before Starmer arrived at Number 10 after which public commentators began to state the same). But if Starmer’s tenure hadn’t been filled with those official matters he bungled, as well as the effects of the US-Iran war on people, he probably would have retained some level of confidence among citizens that could see him to the next election and beyond. Plus, he didn’t strip the highest political office of its dignity with efforts to appear like everyone else.

Meanwhile, if everyday living is tough for the electorates they consider such things before they remember their PM has been a likeable fellow. My observation is that citizens respect political leaders more when they get things done while surrounding their office with some level of distance and mystery. What is insufferable is a leader who focuses on being approachable but doesn’t get things done. There are many uncomplimentary tags for such a situation, and Burnham has no need to invite them in the period citizens’ patience permits him to stay on this job. He should concentrate more on resolving issues that hit citizens hard, rather than stripping leadership of all allures that most folks still admire.
news.summary:
Exploring political populism and whether UK PM Andy Burnham’s ‘everyday folks’ approach is a genuine leadership style or a calculated move to win votes.

news.title: Copper prices drift lower
news.text:
LONDON: Copper prices fell on Thursday after Reuters reported the White House has yet to decide on refined copper tariffs as officials assess concerns that higher prices could raise manufacturing costs. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange fell 3.1percent to USD14,312 a metric ton by 1039 GMT after touching a record high of USD14,875 earlier in the session.

COMEX October copper futures slid 4.2percent to USD6.5355 per lb, or USD14,408 per ton, reducing the premium over the LME prices. The US administration under President Donald Trump is under pressure ahead of mid-term elections in November to demonstrate that its policies are lowering costs for American consumers and businesses.

“That update most certainly sent the cat in among the pigeons,” said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, referring to Reuters’ report.

Copper, widely used in power and construction, has gained 16percent this year as metal flowed into US warehouses ahead of potential tariffs on refined copper imports, stoking concerns over availability in traditional consuming regions.

Copper stocks in the COMEX warehouses have reached a record high of 696,259 tons after months of inflows. “Whether these inventories ultimately become stranded, or eventually return to the global market if no tariffs are introduced, may help determine whether current price levels are sustainable,” Hansen said.

After the Reuters’ report was published on Thursday, the premium of the LME cash contract over the three-month benchmark sank to a discount for the first time since late July. The discount was last at USD13.5 a ton, indicating reduced concerns about a shortage of near-term supplies.

Among other LME metals, aluminium fell 1.5percent to USD3,308 a ton, zinc slid 2.2percent to USD3,962.50, lead eased 0.4percent to USD1,907, tin lost 0.2percent to USD54,845 and nickel was down 0.9percent at USD16,740.

news.title: Trump promises Americans USD5,000 if Republicans win Congress
news.text:
DALLAS: President Donald Trump on Wednesday promised USD5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, coupling the extraordinary claim with a plea for his supporters to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get USD5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend,” he told the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, as the party struggles in polls against the Democrats.

The president did not disclose where the money would come from — with the theoretical bill likely topping USD1 trillion — saying only that “our country is making so much money.”

Doubling down on his bet that he can help Republicans defy opinion polls and retain both houses of Congress on November 3, Trump said: “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

“I’m on the ballot, I’m on the ballot — just one more time,” he told the crowd.

Opinion polls overwhelmingly show that Trump’s approval ratings are in the low 30s, as voters become increasingly angry about high prices and the war he launched against Iran.

Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favor in November.

news.title: Nigeria gets AGOA extension, urged to boost exports
news.text:
The Nigerian-American Chamber of Commerce has urged Nigeria to use the extension of the African Growth and Opportunity Act to expand non-oil exports and address domestic bottlenecks limiting access to the United States market.

The call followed the signing by United States President Donald Trump of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, which extends AGOA through December 31, 2028.

The extension preserves duty-free access to the US market for Nigeria and 31 other sub-Saharan African countries, providing businesses with greater certainty to plan investments, production and exports.

The measure passed the United States Senate by 90 votes to six and the House of Representatives by 340 votes to 54.

The Chamber disclosed this in a statement issued on Thursday and signed by its Deputy President, Nigerian-American Chamber of Commerce, Ehi Braimah.

The NACC National President, Alhaji Sheriff Balogun, said the extension provided Nigeria with an opportunity to strengthen its export base and attract new investment.

“This extension gives Nigeria the certainty needed to invest and expand our exports. But we must use these twenty-eight months to move beyond oil. Nigeria is the second-largest AGOA beneficiary, yet we’re underutilising it. We need to diversify into agricultural products, textiles, processed foods and manufactures where we have real advantage.”

The Chamber said the extension should be used to address structural challenges that have limited Nigeria’s ability to maximise preferential access to the US market. It called on the Federal Government, private sector and state governments to take coordinated and practical measures during the extension period.

The NACC urged stakeholders to broaden Nigeria’s AGOA exports beyond crude oil by developing agricultural products, textiles, processed foods and manufactured goods capable of competing in the US market.

It also called for the removal of domestic bottlenecks affecting exporters, particularly challenges involving ports, standards compliance and logistics, which can delay shipments, raise costs and weaken the competitiveness of Nigerian businesses.

The Chamber further encouraged the Nigerian government to engage with Washington on trade-related concerns, including issues surrounding forced-labour compliance, to protect Nigeria’s continued access to the US market and strengthen confidence between both countries. 

It said greater continental coordination would also be important, urging Nigeria to work with the African Union and the African Continental Free Trade Area framework to strengthen Africa’s collective position in discussions on the modernisation and future of AGOA.

The NACC also advocated stronger US-Nigeria commercial partnerships through joint ventures, technology transfer and increased investment in productive sectors of the Nigerian economy.

Balogun said Nigeria needed to make urgent use of the extension period. “The next two years are a sprint, not a pause. NACC will connect Nigerian producers with American buyers and make the business case for a lasting successor to AGOA that serves all our interests.”

The Chamber said it would continue to facilitate commercial relationships between Nigerian producers and American buyers while supporting businesses seeking to understand and access opportunities under AGOA.

It said Nigeria’s position as one of the leading beneficiaries of AGOA provided a foundation for expanding non-oil exports and strengthening the country’s participation in international trade.

The Chamber added that increased exports of value-added Nigerian products could contribute to job creation, industrial development, foreign exchange earnings and broader economic growth.

As the United States and African countries consider the future of trade relations beyond the current AGOA extension, the NACC said Nigeria must demonstrate that it can make productive use of the remaining period while contributing to discussions on a sustainable successor framework.

The Chamber therefore called for coordinated efforts involving government, businesses, exporters, manufacturers, farmers, financial institutions and other relevant stakeholders to ensure that Nigeria enters the next phase of US-Africa trade from a stronger position.

The NACC said it remained committed to promoting bilateral trade and investment between Nigeria and the United States and providing its members and partners with advocacy, market intelligence, trade facilitation and networking opportunities.

The Nigerian-American Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1960, is Nigeria’s foremost bilateral chamber of commerce promoting trade and investment relations between Nigeria and the United States.

With its headquarters in Lagos and chapters across Nigeria and in the United States, including Maryland and Houston, the Chamber provides advocacy, trade facilitation, market intelligence, and networking services to its members and partners.
news.summary:
Nigeria has received an AGOA extension. The Nigerian-American Chamber of Commerce urges the country to boost non-oil exports and fix trade bottlenecks.

news.title: JD Vance takes center stage at Republican midterm convention as the party faces midterm risks
news.text: Republicans opened the second and final day of their midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday knowing that history is not on their side this election season, but counting on President Donald Trump to propel voters to protect their House and Senate majorities.They're also setting the stage for what could come next in a post-Trump era, as Vice President JD Vance takes the primetime speaking slot just ahead of the president and following a tribute to Charlie Kirk, the conservative leader who was assassinated one year ago. Vance has not said whether he will run for the White House, and Trump has yet to name an heir apparent.With Republican control of Congress at risk this November and the next presidential election two years away, voters are still assessing their options.“We’ve got a deep bench,” said Bruce Johnston, 62, who drove 29 hours with his son from Delaware to be in Dallas. “I mean you’ve got a lot of good candidates. I’d pick any of those for the primary. And we’ll get a good one.”His son, Anthony, 33, said he believes Vance is being groomed as Trump's successor.“No one’s Trump,” he said. “But I like him a lot.”RELATED STORY | 'Pretend that I'm on the ballot': Trump courts Republicans at unusual GOP midterm conventionRepublicans hope to avoid midterm losses in NovemberMore immediately, however, Republicans face a potential reckoning this fall.They are struggling to bolster enthusiasm for congressional GOP candidates and laboring to overcome voters’ concerns about the economy and the war with Iran. While many Republicans skipped the confab at American Airlines Center, others still see solidarity with Trump as their best shot at winning, despite the president’s low approval rating.They spent the first night denouncing Democrats as extremists and Trump capped Wednesday by making the outlandish promise of $5,000 to each American adult if his party wins. Such a proposal could cost more than $1 trillion and was roundly panned by budget experts — and even some Republicans in the president's party.“The midterms are not supposed to be won by the sitting president,” Trump acknowledged during a lengthy primetime speech.But he framed the election as a referendum and encouraged voters to cast their ballots as if they were voting for him: “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”House Democrats, in Texas for a second day of counterprogramming, blasted the Republicans’ convention as an opulent spectacle for an out-of-touch president.“As Donald Trump and JD Vance party away for two days, the average American family can’t afford the groceries,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. “Donald Trump does not care about the average American family or about affordability.”Protesters chanting “say it loud, say it clear, Donald Trump’s not welcome here” marched down streets, but were stopped by police from getting too close to the site.RELATED STORY | Trump says Iran War will end after the midterm electionsRepublicans are showcasing accomplishments and eyeing 2028Vance’s keynote will be closely watched for any hints about his political aspirations. The vice president has demurred on whether he will run for president in 2028, but he’s widely expected to run.Chants of “JD, JD, JD” broke out at Vance’s meeting with delegates from presidential battleground states Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin and his home state of Ohio, according to one attendee.The vice president, who also serves as the Republican National Committee’s finance chair, raised $2 million for the party earlier Thursday at a fundraiser in Dallas, according to a person familiar with the event who was not authorized to discuss it publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.The second night of the convention showcased some of the most electorally endangered Republicans in Congress and those challenging Democrats in tough races, as well as another potential presidential hopeful: Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who railed against liberal Democrats.“We must stand and defeat the communists,” Cruz thundered to cheers. “We must stay America.”Coming on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, the evening marked that moment, as the crowd waved American flag placards. It also produced a video tribute to Kirk, who co-founded the conservative group Turning Point USA and was assassinated on this day last year at an event in Utah.“His voice has only grown louder,” said Lucas Miles, a pastor and vice president at Turning Point. “Charlie is gone, but the mission lives on.”The night's themes delved into what House Speaker Mike Johnson calls the “Contrast for America,” as Republicans showcased what they call their “Big Beautiful Bill” of tax breaks and spending cuts, and warned of a bleak future if Democrats take control.The campaign slogan is a throwback to another Republican leader, Newt Gingrich, offered a Contract with America. This time, rather than presenting a detailed list of priorities, Republicans are drawing a contrast with the Democrats, who they contend are too far left and would focus on investigating the Trump administration.Republicans have been quick to portray all Democrats as in line with their most liberal candidates, particularly a new generation, some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America."It truly is a contrast between common sense and crazy," Johnson said. "We cannot and we will not allow them to take the majority in Congress."Trump hopes the convention will help GOP buck historical trendsWith the Republican majorities in the House and Senate both at risk this fall, the president’s agenda for his final two years in office is also at stake. The margins in Congress are expected to be narrow, with a few seats in a shrunken map of competitive races determining the outcome.Presidents past have acknowledged their midterm losses — Barack Obama called his 2010 setbacks a “shellacking,” George W. Bush labeled his a “thumping.”But Trump often refuses to accept defeat, including his false claims that he, rather than Joe Biden, won the 2020 election. One of the many people he pardoned for their actions in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, former Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes, appeared at the convention.Trump on Wednesday predicted that “the great American majority is going to stand up and continue to Make America Great Again. And we will make our voices heard, perhaps like never before.”
news.summary: Republicans opened the second and final day of their midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday knowing that history is not on their side this election season.

news.title: Democratic Rep tells ABC, CBS to 'grow a spine' after Kimmel announces alternative Talarico interview
news.text: Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., attacked ABC, CBS and other networks in a pair of deleted X posts on Thursday after hearing reports about Jimmy Kimmel's upcoming interview with Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico. The late-night host announced Wednesday night that he would be interviewing Talarico, but out of concern for the FCC under President Donald Trump, he added that he would be releasing the interview on YouTube instead of airing it on his show, "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" Lieu accused ABC and other networks, like CBS, of "bending the knee" to authoritarians by refusing to air interviews of elected officials. JIMMY KIMMEL RETURNS FROM LENGTHY HIATUS WITH DEFIANT MESSAGE TO FCC CHAIR BRENDAN CARR "Dear @ABC, @CBS and other networks: Grow a f---ing spine. Air whatever interviews with elected officials you want. You will win in court. Bending the knee to an authoritarian Administration only makes things worse. I assume you will now never air an interview of Trump as well?" Lieu wrote. He also wrote, "You know what else you can do @ABC and @CBS? Offer Ken Paxton the opportunity to come onto late night talk shows where the hosts can legitimately skewer Paxton by asking him about all his scandals. But instead you groveled and chose the path of self-censorship. Shameful." Fox News Digital reached out to ABC, CBS and Lieu's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Kimmel similarly accused the FCC of targeting his show and ABC based on "guest bookings it would seem they don’t like." DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS "Now that he’s president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on traditional simple editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like. And so, out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV," Kimmel said. The situation was reminiscent of former late-night host Stephen Colbert's interview with Talarico ahead of the Texas Senate primary, in which he competed against Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett. Colbert's show, which has since been canceled, did not air the interview with Talarico and only posted it to the show's YouTube channel in February. Colbert announced at the time that CBS had stopped them from airing the interview. However, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr clarified to Fox News at the time that the interview would have potentially violated the equal-time rule, which requires broadcast stations to provide equal opportunities to opposing political candidates during an election season. COLBERT LASHES OUT AT CBS, SAYS CANCELLATION ‘REINFORCED A NARRATIVE’ OF ‘KNEE BENDING’ TO TRUMP In a comment to Fox News Digital, Curtis Houck, managing editor at NewsBusters, suggested Kimmel could land in "hot water" for his stunt to move around the equal-time rule and avoid speaking with Talarico's GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Jimmy Kimmel thinks he's being cute or even brave by thumbing his nose at the FCC, but he's likely to end up in hot water for this. The equal time rules are what they are. Kimmel and his clapping seals in the liberal, elitist media are telling on themselves when they try to explain away the record of Kimmel and his fellow network late-night hosts as virulent partisans with guest disparities that can only be rivaled by ABC's 'The View,'" Houck said. news.title: Zelensky Says He Plans to Meet Trump in New York in Late September
news.text:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that he expects to meet US President Donald Trump in New York later this month as Washington renews efforts to move stalled talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine forward.

Speaking at a press conference in Canada, Zelensky said discussions with the US side would continue during his visit to New York.

“At the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelensky said.

He indicated that the meeting with Trump could provide greater clarity on the next steps in the diplomatic process.

“I think that... I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump,” he said.

Zelensky added that Ukrainian and US negotiators remained in constant contact and that he hoped for progress on energy and grain talks following the planned meeting.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said Thursday that he had spoken with Trump “a couple of times” recently about Russia’s war against Ukraine as well as the conflict involving Iran.

Carney said the conversations reflected Canada’s responsibility to continue working with Washington despite tensions between the two countries, but gave no details about the discussions.
news.summary: Zelensky says he expects to meet Trump in New York later this month, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he has also recently discussed Ukraine with the US president.

news.text:

"They're trying to do anything possible to get me out because they think the Democrats will let them essentially have a nuclear weapon. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon," Trump told Fox News in an interview.

The US leader also argued that Tehran would have already possessed nukes, had he not moved to withdraw from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), or the Iran nuclear deal negotiated by the 44th US President, Barack Obama. "I terminated the worst agreement I've ever seen - the Obama nuclear deal, the JCPOA. What a horrible agreement! That was a road to a nuclear weapon," he maintained.

news.title: Pete Hegseth's Approval Hits Record Low Amid 2028 Speculation
news.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's approval rating has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded by Quinnipiac University, according to a new poll released Thursday, as questions about his political future continue to surface despite his repeated denials that he is considering a 2028 presidential run. The survey found that 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job as Secretary of Defense, while 57 percent disapprove. Another 11 percent did not offer an opinion. Quinnipiac said the result marks the worst approval rating Hegseth has received in its polling. His previous low was 34 percent, recorded in surveys released in May and July. The poll also found that 39 percent of voters are either very confident or somewhat confident in Hegseth's leadership of the U.S. military, while 56 percent said they were either not so confident or not confident at all. Newsweek reached out to the Pentagon and White House on Thursday evening. Confidence Gap Widens The findings arrive at a difficult moment for Hegseth, who has remained one of the most scrutinized members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet. Questions about his leadership have persisted amid the administration's military operations in Iran and the fallout from the Signal chat controversy over discussions of planned strikes in Yemen last year. Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth, recently declared that the defense secretary had "lost my confidence," citing concerns about his management style and Pentagon leadership. Recent criticism has extended beyond Tillis. Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall told ABC News' This Week on Sunday that he had "never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth," arguing that the removal of senior officers and intervention in promotions had created a climate in which military leaders are reluctant to speak candidly. Hegseth's supporters reject that characterization. In comments previously provided to Newsweek, Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell called suggestions that the Defense Department is in disarray "completely baseless" and said the Pentagon is "firing on all cylinders under Secretary Hegseth's leadership." Such criticism nevertheless appears to have taken a toll on his standing with voters. While Hegseth remains a favorite among many Trump supporters, the new Quinnipiac numbers suggest he continues to struggle with the broader electorate. The survey was released as Trump's own approval rating remained underwater, with 33 percent approving and 59 percent disapproving of the president's job performance. 2028 Questions Persist The poll comes less than two weeks after Hegseth denied a report that he was considering a bid for the White House in 2028. In late August, NBC News reported that Hegseth had discussed a possible presidential campaign with friends and associates. Hegseth quickly rejected the report, calling it "100% false," while Parnell told Newsweek that the secretary's sole focus was leading the War Department. Although Hegseth has denied considering a White House bid, he previously ran unsuccessfully for the U.S. Senate in Minnesota in 2012 before joining Fox News and later entering the Trump administration. Even so, speculation about the post-Trump Republican field has continued. During a September 8 appearance on CNN's The Source, Republican Senator Ted Cruz was asked by Kaitlan Collins about potential Republican contenders for 2028. While stressing that Republicans should focus on the upcoming midterm elections, Cruz listed several figures who "may run," including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Tulsi Gabbard, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Hegseth. Trump has also weighed in on the speculation. Asked earlier this month about reports that Hegseth was considering a 2028 bid, Trump said the defense secretary was "doing a fantastic job" but added that it was "very early" to discuss the next presidential race. "Right now, all he loves and all he cares about is the military and taking care of the military," Trump said. For now, Hegseth continues to insist he has no plans to run. But as Republicans increasingly look toward 2028, the new Quinnipiac poll highlights a potential challenge he would face if that ever changed: persuading a broader electorate at a time when his approval ratings are at a record low. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Pete Hegseth's approval rating falls to a Quinnipiac record low as 2028 speculation continues.
news.author: Steve Mollman

news.title: Mourners honor Charlie Kirk at Turning Point Phoenix headquarters one year after death
news.text:
Ashlee Rivera used to watch every single one of Charlie Kirk’s videos. So on the anniversary of his assassination, she couldn’t help but cry. 

“He was just such a great person and just a tremendous loss. He really loved our country,” she said through tears.

Rivera was among the mourners who came to the Turning Point USA headquarters in Ahwatukee Foothills to mark the Sept. 10 anniversary of his murder. 

It’s been one year since Kirk was shot and killed at age 31 at a Turning Point event on a Utah campus. The moment shocked the nation and shone a light on the country’s tense political divide. 

“It really opened our eyes. I think it made us see how divided we were and how differently half of us think,” said Andrea Montierth, who lives in Bowling Green, Kentucky, and attended the memorial virtually on a FaceTime call with Rivera, a Phoenix resident. 

Kirk was the co-founder of Turning Point USA, a conservative powerhouse that blended political organizing, media and fundraising to become a force during the Trump era. Kirk was known for sharing his controversial views on the popular “The Charlie Kirk Show” podcast and by debating liberal students on college campuses. 

His family, friends and supporters marked the anniversary of his murder with events around the country. 

Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, was honored by President Donald Trump the evening of Sept. 9 at the Republican midterm convention in Texas. A statue of Kirk was unveiled in New York City’s Times Square. Turning Point leaders returned to the site of his death for an event at Utah Valley University. Vice President JD Vance called into “The Charlie Kirk Show" to pay his respects.

Meanwhile at the Ahwatukee headquarters where Kirk built his conservative empire, mourners came to remember Kirk and reflect on his life.

Signs lined the closed-down road to Turning Point’s offices with photos of Kirk and messages like “NEVER SURRENDER” and “IT’S OK TO LOVE YOUR COUNTRY." At the front gate, people passed through metal detectors and left flowers in front of a poster of the slain Turning Point leader. 

That included Jana Cunningham, who brought her 2-year-old son, William, to honor Kirk with a bouquet.

“I see Charlie Kirk as such an amazing leader and an influential American. I want my son to eventually grow up and know that as well,” said Cunningham, who lives in Mesa.

Several people declined interviews through tears, saying they were too emotional to speak. April Flores of Yuma placed a bouquet of flowers outside the building and cried. 

Turning Point blended remembering Kirk with political organizing. Staff members were on hand to register voters as part of the group’s “Fly the Flag” drive. “CHARLIE WANTS YOU TO REGISTER TO VOTE,” read a large banner that depicted Kirk in blue and white. 

Staff handed out white “FREEDOM” T-shirts, a replica of the shirt Kirk was wearing when he was killed. The shirts quickly became a popular symbol of support in the days after he was assassinated. 

The shirt was also preserved in bronze. Leaders unveiled a statue by the artist Quintin McCann that morning, which depicted Kirk tossing baseball caps in his “FREEDOM” T-shirt, a cross hanging from his neck. U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Arizona, whom Kirk endorsed for governor, delivered remarks.

The anniversary was personal for Anna Rockey, a 24-year-old nurse. She and her husband had looked up to Kirk and watched his videos daily. They both cried when they found out he had been killed. 

So when Rockey’s husband was offered a job at Turning Point in the spring, the couple packed their bags and moved from Virginia to Phoenix.

“My husband realized that he wanted to change the world, I mean do something meaningful instead of just working a 9 to 5 that doesn't have an impact on our country. So that's why we moved,” Rockey said.

While Rockey came to the Phoenix headquarters, her husband spent the anniversary at the Utah event. Rockey said she recently toured Turning Point's offices and was impressed to learn how much work the group does through its faith and student outreach programs. 

Turning Point’s campus chapters swelled after he was killed, and more churches and pastors joined Turning Point Faith, according to a memo from the organization. 

“Obviously it’s a tragedy, but I think the Lord knew what he was doing, and I think that at the end of the day, the Lord is sovereign and he felt that Charlie's death could do more for the country than if he were to be alive still. And I think it really has made people just think and you know, kind of reconnect with God and realize what's truly important in life,” Rockey said. 

Mourners also left with American flags and copies of Kirk’s book, “Stop, in the Name of God: Why Honoring the Sabbath Will Transform Your Life,” which was published posthumously last year. 

A semitruck carting a mobile In-N-Out Burger trailer was parked in front of the campus. Nearby, another trailer wrapped with a picture of Charlie and Erika Kirk featured a large TV screen playing Turning Point videos. 

The memorial drew out-of-town visitors like Anita Bartlett and Gabe St. Clair, who came to pay tribute to Kirk while they waited to catch a flight back to Oklahoma. 

“It's just such a travesty,” Bartlett said. “I took a picture and did a video as we were walking in because it just, if I wasn't doing something to occupy my mind, I probably would have been crying the whole time walking in.”

Bartlett has two college-age daughters and said she admired the work that Kirk did to promote conservative values on campus. 

“My youngest daughter, she really learned a lot from him,” Bartlett said. “She was so sad when all this happened.” 

Others happened upon the event by chance. 

Ray Hightower was working nearby when he noticed a Turning Point sign and decided to come to the memorial. He said it is important for people to start listening to each other instead of resorting to violence. 

“When we do that, we find that the people we disagree with are not necessarily the evil rat bastards we think that they are,” Hightower said. 

Kirk had been a familiar face in Hightower’s YouTube feed before he was killed. Hightower found it interesting to watch Kirk’s evolution over the years, saying the activist’s debate style became “tempered with diplomacy” as he got older. 

Hightower acknowledged that many people have a negative impression of Kirk and what he stood for during his life. Kirk made controversial comments on issues such as race, gender and guns, which circulated online after he was killed. 

“I don't blame them,” Hightower said. “The people who have negative impressions of Charlie Kirk probably haven't listened to his videos.” 

A look back 1 year after death: What did Charlie Kirk say and believe?

That feeling was echoed by Elizabeth Fila, a Laveen resident who had been following Kirk for years before he was killed. Fila fled communist Poland with her parents when she was 6 years old, she said. 

Fila’s family is politically divided. Her adult children send her clips of Kirk’s incendiary comments, but Fila feels they are missing the full picture of what he stood for. When Fila wears her Kirk T-shirt, her youngest child gets scared because of the reaction she will get from high school classmates, she said.

“This man wasn't doing anything wrong. He was just voicing his truth opinion, and he was bold enough and brave enough to do so,” Fila said. “It's sad that so many people have such a negative reaction towards somebody who just wanted to spread positivity and enforce religion and just the principles of this country.” 

Stephanie Murray covers national politics and the Trump administration for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. She co-hosts “The Gaggle,” The Republic’s weekly politics podcast. Reach her at stephanie.murray@usatodayco.com, on X and TikTok @stephanie_murr and on Instagram @stephaniemurray.news.

news.title: Two arrested at socialist anti-Trump protest after assault at ‘closest entry point’ to GOP convention: police
news.text: A socialist "Never Trumpers" protester blamed "conservative provocateurs" for a tense confrontation with police that resulted in multiple arrests just outside the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas. Videos posted on social media Thursday afternoon showed what appeared to be hundreds of 'Never Trumpers' confronting Dallas police just blocks from where the president was set to deliver his convention closing speech. Authorities responded with a strong show of force that included officers in apparent riot gear. The Dallas Police Department confirmed with Fox News Digital that two protesters were arrested on charges related to their actions during the protest. The department said that officers assigned to the area arrested the two protesters after it said they "assaulted a counter-protester" and "obstructed a road." The department said the suspects’ names and specific charges will be released after they are booked into jail. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION Fox News Digital spoke with a protester named Rick Majumdar, who was wearing a shirt with the initials for the "Freedom Road Socialist Organization" (FRSO), which, according to its website, is a "national organization of revolutionaries fighting for socialism in the United States." Majumdar said that the protest was organized by the "Dallas Against the Trump Agenda Coalition," which he said consists of 16 "faith-based organizations, pro-immigrants’ rights groups and labor organizations." "We're here to protest the Republican agenda, the Trump agenda and all its policies that it has enacted over the last few years," he explained, adding, "The march is an important event, we feel, against this convention that's happening for the last two days." REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG He said that during the group's march "we encountered some street closures by the police" and that officers arrested a couple of protesters who "were at the front of the group." Pressed on why the protesters were arrested, Majumdar said: "Those people were trying to draw people away from rioting provocateurs, and I think the police heard something and they immediately tackled two of them and arrested them and some of them even pulled out their guns as well." The protest came amid heightened concerns over political violence and the targeting of public figures. It also coincided with the first anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point USA co-founder Charlie Kirk. CHARLIE KIRK CONTINUES TO INSPIRE REPUBLICANS AS PARTY RALLIES FOR MIDTERM BATTLE: 'HAVE COURAGE' SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Majumdar did not answer whether the protesters blocked any roads but said the confrontation occurred at the "closest entry point" to the convention. news.title: US Appeal Court affirms block on Trump bid to curb mail-in ballots
news.text:
A US appeals court on Thursday upheld a lower court’s block on President Donald Trump’s executive order curbing the use of mail-in ballots in November’s midterm elections.

District Judge Indira Talwani issued a preliminary injunction last week barring the US Postal Service (USPS) from carrying out a plan that critics say would restrict distribution of mail-in ballots.

A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit unanimously upheld Talwani’s injunction, which the Trump administration has already appealed to the Supreme Court.

The judges said they agreed with the district court’s conclusion that carrying out the executive order “will likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud.”

A coalition of Democratic-ruled states sued the administration on the grounds that under the US Constitution, states — and not the federal government — retain broad control over elections.

North Carolina began sending mail-in ballots to voters last week and other states have also begun to do so.

Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting, saying without evidence that it is vulnerable to fraud.

Trump’s order would require the compilation of lists of eligible voters and for the USPS to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists.

A USPS whistleblower has warned that millions of Americans may not receive ballots because the systems being used by the postal service have been put together in a “sloppy and rushed manner.”

Trump has long been a critic of mail-in ballots but has frequently used them himself, including last month when he voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary.

The president has for years claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is highly vulnerable to fraud, repeatedly linking it to his false assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden.

Polls show that Trump’s Republican Party faces a serious threat of losing its narrow control of Congress in November, particularly the House of Representatives.

If Democrats win, they have signaled they would block Trump’s agenda and could even move to impeach him for the third time.
